blogs.title: Beyond the Right‑to‑Control Theory: Why the Supreme Court’s Fraud Doctrine Is Revolutionary
blogs.description: This post dives into the Supreme Court’s landmark decisions in Ciminelli and Kousisis, examining how the Court re‑defined the fraudulent‑inducement theory to protect money and property rather than intangible economic information. It explains why the Fifth Circuit’s ruling in *United States v. Constantinescu* follows that logic, how it impacts securities fraud prosecutions, and what it means for defendants who manipulate investors online.

blogs.title: From Indictment to Trial: Why the Fifth Circuit Overturned a Dismissal in a Pump‑and‑Dump Scheme
blogs.description: Here we unpack the procedural and substantive standards for an indictment’s sufficiency. Drawing on *U.S. v. Rafoi* and *U.S. v. Fontenot*, the article details how the circuit applied the mail‑and‑wire fraud analogies to securities fraud elements, corrected the district court’s error, and what this reversal signals for prosecutors and defendants in future fraud cases.

blogs.title: Digital Wall Street: Social‑Media Influencers and the New Frontier of Securities Fraud
blogs.description: This analysis looks at the rise of influencer‑driven pump‑and‑dump schemes, with *Constantinescu* as a case study. It discusses how large online followings and real‑time messaging create novel markets, the regulatory challenges posed by this new frontier, and the potential for new oversight or free‑speech defenses in the digital era.

blogs.title: Indictment Dismissals and Double Jeopardy: Lessons from the Constantinescu Reversal
blogs.description: Focusing on the constitutional dimension, this post explores when a district court can validly dismiss an indictment for failure to state a claim, the de‑novo review standard used by the Fifth Circuit, and the double‑jeopardy implications of a reversal. It highlights practical takeaways for prosecutorial strategy and defendants facing similar procedural hurdles.
